source_caption:
Currently the highest-rated film on Letterboxd, Harakiri is a samurai film that slowly turns a story about honour into something much darker. Masaki Kobayashi’s 1962 classic follows a ronin who arrives at a feudal clan’s estate asking to commit seppuku, but what follows exposes the hypocrisy and cruelty hiding behind the samurai code.

The film is also visually incredible, with Yoshio Miyajima’s stark black-and-white cinematography making its compositions, empty spaces and long silences feel almost as important as the action. Its influence even extends to games like Ghost of Tsushima, whose developers specifically studied Harakiri’s famous duel for the game’s own tense, slow-building sword fights. More than 60 years later, it still feels remarkably modern.

🎥: Harakiri (1962)
Dir. Masaki Kobayashi

source_details.title: Harakiri
source_details.synopsis: Harakiri (Japanese: 切腹, Hepburn: Seppuku) is a 1962 Japanese jidaigeki film directed by Masaki Kobayashi. The story takes place between 1619 and 1630 during the Edo period and the rule of the Tokugawa shogunate. It tells the story of the rōnin Hanshirō Tsugumo, who requests to commit seppuku (harakiri) within the manor of a local feudal lord, using the opportunity to explain the events that drove him to ask for death before an audience of samurai. The film continues to receive critical acclaim, often considered one of the greatest films of all time.
